target_customer: Small and medium e-commerce sellers needing cash to buy inventory, with investors buying confirmed invoices
problem: E-commerce companies pay for inventory months before it sells. Kickpay let them post confirmed invoices to a marketplace where investors bought them, so sellers received most of the value upfront.
business_model: Marketplace taking a cut from sellers and investors (no fees at the March 2015 launch)

founders.name: Andrew McCalister
education: University of Cambridge, master's in Engineering and Management
Bachelor's double major in Mechanical Engineering and Industrial Design (institution not named)
founders.background_notes: Per YC page; TechCrunch 2015-03-20 says he came up with the idea while at Heyzap and is originally from Scotland.

founders.name: Stefano Bernardi
founders.background_notes: Betable per TechCrunch 2015-03-20; YC page notes he later became a GP at Unruly Capital.

founders.name: Sean Watters
founders.background_notes: Employers per TechCrunch 2015-03-20; YC page lists him as Founder/CTO.

investors: Angel investors including former PayPal, Mint and Palantir executives

technical_complexity.rationale: Needed accounting and bank data integrations (QuickBooks) and a rate-setting model, which TechCrunch says used a partnership with Wells Fargo data, plus marketplace and compliance plumbing.

defensibility.rationale: Underwriting data on borrowers could improve over time, but lending marketplaces were copyable and capital supply, not software, was the constraint.

takeover_risk_then.outcome: TechCrunch described the offline factoring market as cumbersome. No source found on any incumbent copying or acquiring Kickpay.

market_need_then: TechCrunch (2015-03-20) cited an estimated 3 trillion dollar worldwide market for the concept offline and reported more than 1 million dollars provided to companies during a two month invite-only beta.

branding.domain_note: Used kickpay.com, per the YC page

brand_strength.rationale: Covered by TechCrunch at launch but no press on the brand itself. The name is easily confused with Kickfurther, a separate inventory financing company, and with later companies using the Kickpay name.

outcome_analysis: Kickpay launched in March 2015 with an invoice financing marketplace and more than 1 million dollars of early financing volume, backed by angel money and YC. Directories list it as inactive or closed but no shutdown post-mortem, acquisition or dated closure was found, so the cause is not public. Later companies with similar names and Kickfurther appear in results but are different entities.
notes: kickpay.com returned HTTP 503, so the site is treated as unreachable. TechCrunch gives no angel amount. CB Insights shows a $120K seed (single database); Seedtable lists seed dates of 2014-12 and 2015-07 without amounts, and CB Insights appears to mix some figures with Kickfurther, so the amount is unverified. YC page lists three founders although team size is 2. No competitor was named in the TechCrunch launch article and the Kickfurther sources found are dated 2016 or later, which is too late for this batch, so the list is empty.
